Thomas Adams
AD-amz
proper noun
From the English surname Adams; the early-seventeenth-century preacher called the Shakespeare of the Puritans.

📖 Biblical Definition

Thomas Adams was an English preacher of the early seventeenth century, so vivid and pointed in his sermons, so rich in image and so searching in application, that later readers called him the Shakespeare of the Puritans. He preached the Scriptures with a quick eye for the deceitfulness of the human heart and a plain aim at the conscience, sparing no sin and flattering no sinner. His sermons and his great commentary on the Second Epistle of Peter are a treasury of pungent, Scriptural, soul-searching divinity. The dictionary honours Adams as a master of the preacher’s art set wholly in the service of the word, which is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit (Heb 4:12). He took heed to the more sure word of prophecy, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place (2Pe 1:19), and trusted that it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe (1Co 1:21). His wit was never the display of the preacher but the servant of the truth, a sword to cut and a light to show; and he preached the word in season and out of season, reproving, rebuking, and exhorting with all longsuffering and doctrine (2Ti 4:2). Adams stands among the great Puritan preachers whose eloquence was the handmaid of holiness.

An early-seventeenth-century English preacher called the Shakespeare of the Puritans for his vivid, searching sermons.

THOMAS ADAMS, an English preacher of the early seventeenth century.

📖 Key Scripture

2Pe 1:19 — "We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:"

Heb 4:12 — "For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart."

1Co 1:21 — "For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe."

2Ti 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

His eloquence was the handmaid of holiness, the preacher’s art set wholly in the service of the searching word.

expand to see more

What is honourable in Thomas Adams is the marriage of eloquence and faithfulness. His vivid wit and searching images were never spent on the display of the preacher but on the cutting of the conscience and the exalting of Christ. The dictionary honours him as a master of the preacher’s art who kept that art wholly the servant of the word, which is sharper than any twoedged sword.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the gifts of the preacher are the handmaids of holiness, not its rivals. The age loves eloquence for its own sake and tolerates much that flatters the sinner; Adams flattered none, but took heed to the sure word of prophecy as a light in a dark place, and trusted God to save by the foolishness of preaching. His example rebukes both the dull preaching that neglects the gifts God gives and the showy preaching that spends them on itself; the true preacher, like Adams, makes his every power a sword for the truth and a light for the soul.
